WEEK 1 LAB · FILES, RULES, AND RELATIONSHIPS
:::

# What does this representation permit?

A tidy-looking file can still permit contradictory, incomplete, or ambiguous states. In this lab, you will make those weaknesses visible before proposing a better model.

::: {.lesson-question}
**Lab question:** Which assumptions are carried only by the people using the file, and which should become explicit parts of a data system?
:::
:::

::: {.activity-meta-grid}
::: {.activity-meta-card}
### Time

Approximately 35–45 minutes
:::

::: {.activity-meta-card}
### Collaboration

Groups of two or three
:::

::: {.activity-meta-card}
### Submission

One short artifact per group
:::
:::

Before beginning, read the Week 1 lecture, [Is a database just a glorified spreadsheet?](../lectures/week-01-database-or-spreadsheet.qmd), through the discussion of spreadsheets and databases.

## Learning goals

By completing this lab, you should be able to:

1. distinguish facts about observations, sites, and sensors;
2. expose update, insertion, and deletion problems in a flat representation;
3. identify rules that the file cannot enforce; and
4. sketch a first model that separates identity, description, and relationships.

## Scenario and data

A field team records stream-temperature observations in one CSV file.

| observation_id | site_code | site_name | sensor_model | observed_at | temperature_c |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---:|
| 1 | CC-01 | Clear Creek | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 09:00 | 8.4 |
| 2 | CC-01 | Clear Creek | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 10:00 | 9.1 |
| 3 | PR-02 | Pine River | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 09:00 | 7.8 |
| 4 | CC-01 | Clear Creak | TempCo T100 | 2026-05-01 11:00 | 9.7 |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Do not clean the data yet

Your goal is to discover what the current representation permits. Correcting row 4 too early would hide the design problem that produced it.
:::

## Part A — Observe

Using the four-row table:

1. Identify every fact that repeats.
2. Mark the row that creates a contradiction and explain the contradiction.
3. List three rules a human reader appears to assume.
4. Identify one useful question the table cannot answer without additional data.

Record your findings in a compact table:

| Observation | Evidence in the file | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |

## Part B — Stress the representation

For each failure below, describe the smallest edit or sequence of edits that would produce it.

| Failure to produce | Minimal change | Why the file cannot prevent it |
|---|---|---|
| Two records identify the same observation | | |
| One site appears under two names | | |
| An observation refers to an unknown sensor | | |
| Deleting a reading removes the only known fact about a site | | |
| Two people make incompatible changes based on the same starting state | | |

## Part C — Propose a model

Sketch boxes for the distinct kinds of things you believe exist. Add a possible identifier to each box and draw the relationships among them. You may draw on paper and attach a clear image, use a diagramming tool, or use Mermaid. Formal ER notation is not required yet.

::: {.activity-checkpoint}
**Checkpoint:** Every box should complete the sentence “This is one _____.” Every line should complete the sentence “One _____ can be related to _____.”
:::

Below your sketch, list at least two assumptions that would need clarification before the design could be considered correct.

## Part D — Defend one rule

Choose one rule that belongs in the data system rather than only in written instructions. State:

1. the rule in plain language;
2. a minimal example that violates it;
3. why the violation matters; and
4. a database mechanism that might enforce it, even if you do not yet know the SQL syntax.

## What to submit

Submit one group artifact containing:

- the names of all participating group members;
- the completed observations from Part A;
- the failure cases from Part B;
- the model sketch and assumptions from Part C; and
- the rule defense from Part D.

The artifact may be a short document, a rendered Quarto page, or a clearly legible scan, as directed by the instructor. A concise submission is expected; completeness and reasoning matter more than visual polish.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Before submitting

Confirm that another group could identify the repeated facts, understand your proposed entities and relationships, and construct the invalid example your chosen rule would reject.
:::

## Completion criteria

A complete submission:

- uses evidence from the supplied rows;
- distinguishes at least three kinds of facts;
- demonstrates multiple ways the flat file can become inconsistent;
- proposes identifiers and relationships rather than merely splitting columns; and
- states assumptions instead of presenting the sketch as the only possible answer.
